We are TerraNova, a group of students from Hof HaCarmel School in Ma’agan Michael, Israel. Our team brings together a wide range of interests and knowledge, including Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Engineering, Mechatronics, Space Science, UX/UI Design, Marine Studies, and Celestial Navigation.

What makes our team special is our combination of innovation.

If you are passionate about science TerraNova is the team for you!
summary:
TerraNova is an interactive web platform that finds the best places on Earth to test equipment, rovers and procedures for lunar and Martian missions. Instead of looking for places that merely look like Mars, it compares real Earth data with published Moon and Mars measurements for the specific conditions a test needs: temperature, solar energy, terrain slope and roughness, dust, aridity, logistics and more.

Users pick a target (Moon or Mars), a mission type and a reference region (such as Gale Crater or the lunar south pole), set weights and hard constraints, and get a global compatibility heatmap on a 3D globe plus a ranked list of the top sites. Every result shows its data sources, a confidence score, an explanation, an execution plan with the best testing season, and a check against NASA's official POWER data.

TerraNova also states clearly what Earth cannot reproduce (vacuum, low gravity, space radiation), so teams know which tests need a laboratory.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraNova helps researchers, engineers and space agencies choose terrestrial analog sites for a specific experiment. The user selects the Moon or Mars, one of 10 mission presets (e.g. lunar polar base, Martian rover testing, dust and abrasion testing) or a custom experiment, a reference region (e.g. Gale Crater, Jezero, Utopia Planitia, lunar south pole), and weights for 25 environmental parameters. TerraNova scores every land cell on Earth (about 357,000 cells on a 0.25° grid), draws a compatibility heatmap on an interactive 3D globe, and ranks the 10 best distinct locations.

HOW IT WORKS

For each location, the score is a weighted average of parameter-specific similarity functions: Gaussian similarity for temperatures, irradiance and wind; log-scale similarity for terrain relief and roughness; and a comparison of whole slope distributions, not just averages. Missing data is never scored as zero; instead a separate data-confidence score shows how complete and reliable each result is. Hard constraints (maximum slope, minimum solar energy, minimum contiguous area, distance to roads, etc.) exclude or flag sites so they can never rank highly by accident. Each parameter is labelled as reproducible outdoors, partially reproducible, laboratory-only or not reproducible on Earth, so vacuum, reduced gravity and space radiation are never given misleading scores.

KEY FEATURES

- Interactive 3D globe (CesiumJS) with overall, per-category, per-parameter, data-confidence and constraint-failure layers

- Detailed location analysis: Earth vs. target comparison table, monthly climate charts, slope and elevation distributions, data-based explanations

- Research advisor: reviews every user input and recommends what is relevant to the research and what is not, based on data coverage, sensitivity and how well the top sites match

- Execution planner: best testing season from monthly climatology, gaps at the site and how to cover them in the lab, and one-click readjustment of climate parameters

- NASA verification: automatically cross-checks the climate values used for scoring against NASA POWER records

- Validation against real analog sites used by NASA and ESA (Atacama, Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, etc.)

- Side-by-side comparison, PDF reports, CSV/GeoJSON/JSON export, interface in English, Hebrew, Spanish and French

DATA

Real open data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 meteorology and CERES solar, 2001–2020 climatology), a global elevation model built from SRTM and other sources, ESA WorldCover land cover, and Natural Earth. Moon and Mars reference values come from published results of NASA missions and instruments (LRO Diviner and LOLA, MGS MOLA, THEMIS, Curiosity REMS and RAD, Perseverance MEDA, InSight, Viking), each with its citation and a label showing whether it is measured, derived or estimated.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy and xarray for the data pipeline and scoring engine; React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS, Recharts and jsPDF for the web interface.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Choosing an analog site is usually based on experience and visual similarity. TerraNova makes the choice transparent, quantitative and specific to the experiment, saving time and money in planning field campaigns and making clear which conditions need laboratory facilities instead.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty was our main design rule: no invented measurements, clear labelling of measured vs. estimated vs. proxy values, a confidence score instead of hiding missing data, and explicit limitations (grid resolution of about 28 km, proxy indices for rock and soil, protected-area data only for the USA).
